title: Regular Expression Matching
pattern: two-dimensional DP over string and pattern positions with a star operator
statement:
Given a string `s` and a pattern `p`, decide whether `p` matches the whole of `s`. Inside `p`, a `.` matches any single character of `s`, and a `*` means zero or more repetitions of the element immediately before it, which is either a letter or a `.`. A `*` with no element before it is ignored, so a `*` at the very start of `p`, or a `*` written directly after another `*`, matches the empty string only and constrains nothing. The match must consume every character of `s` and every element of `p`. Return `true` when `p` matches all of `s` and `false` otherwise.

For example `s = "abc"` and `p = ".*c"` match, while `s = "abc"` and `p = "a*c"` do not.

Constraints: `1 <= s.length <= 10`, `1 <= p.length <= 10`, every character of `s` is `a`, `b` or `c`, and every character of `p` is `a`, `b`, `c`, `.` or `*`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(s: string, p: string)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Decide the state first: which suffix of s and which suffix of the pattern you are matching. Nothing else about the earlier characters matters.
A starred element has exactly two options: skip it and move to the next pattern element, or consume one matching character of s and stay on the same element. An unstarred element has only one.
Compute the table from the ends of both strings towards the front so that every state you need has already been filled in.

editorial.approach: Both solutions first turn the pattern into a list of elements, each one a character (or `.`) with a flag saying whether a `*` follows it; an ignored `*` is simply dropped here, which is what makes the leading and doubled stars harmless. The brute force then matches with plain recursion on the pair of positions `(i, k)`: an unstarred element advances both positions when it matches, and a starred element either skips itself or consumes one more matching character of `s` and stays on the same element. It is correct but re-explores the same `(i, k)` pairs many times, which is exponential. The optimal solution is bottom-up dynamic programming: `dp[i][k]` is true when the suffix `s[i:]` is matched by the elements `k, k+1, ...` of the pattern. The table is filled from `i = n` and `k = m` downwards, so both branches of every transition are already known, and each of the `(n+1)*(m+1)` states costs constant time.
editorial.why_optimal: There are only `(n+1)*(m+1)` distinct pairs of positions, and the answer can depend on every one of them, so O(n*m) states with an O(1) transition is optimal in the worst case; the exponential recursion is exactly this table computed over and over. With `s` and `p` capped at 10 characters the table has at most 121 cells, which is why the hard part of this problem is the recurrence and not the running time.
editorial.pitfalls: Skipping the preprocessing of ignored stars, so a pattern such as `**a` or `*a` either produces a leading star element or crashes while looking at the character before it. Initialising the table wrongly: `dp[n][m]` must be true, and `dp[i][m]` must be false for every `i < n` because an empty pattern cannot match a non-empty string. In the starred transition `dp[i][k] = dp[i][k + 1] or (hit and dp[i + 1][k])`, using `dp[i + 1][k + 1]` in the second branch, which silently allows only a single repetition instead of many. Replacing the repetition with a greedy two-pointer scan, which fails on patterns such as `.*c` against `abc`. Off-by-one on the `i < n` guard used for the character comparison.
